set1.q: How does the visceral pleural line of a pneumothorax appear on a chest radiograph?
opts: A straight, flat line with fluid beneath it and no meniscus is the air-fluid level of a hemopneumothorax, not the visceral pleural line. Tell: free air alone shows a thin, curved line convex toward the chest wall.
Thin, convex toward the chest wall

Correct. The diagnosis is established by the visceral pleural line, the interface of lung and pleural air: thin, sharp lines that are convex outward toward the chest wall. Bronchovascular markings are not typically visible beyond that edge.

Concave margins describe bullae on computed tomography, while pneumothorax lines are convex; that difference separates a large bulla from free pleural air. Tell: a pneumothorax edge bows outward toward the chest wall.
The pleural line is thin and sharp, and bronchovascular markings are not typically visible beyond it. Tell: lung markings continuing past the line argue against free pleural air.

set1.q: Below what volume does a pleural effusion produce no physical exam findings?
opts: Ten milliliters is about the normal pleural fluid volume and the smallest effusion contrast computed tomography may identify. Tell: imaging finds tiny volumes, but the exam stays silent until about 300 mL.
Seventy-five milliliters is enough to blunt the posterior costophrenic angle on an upright film, yet still too small to find on examination. Tell: the film shows 75 mL; the exam needs 300 mL or more.

Correct. Small effusions, under 300 mL, produce no physical exam findings. Larger ones bring asymmetrical expansion, decreased tactile fremitus, dullness and diminished breath sounds, and more than 1000 mL can shift the trachea away from the involved side.
More than 1000 mL is the volume that shifts the trachea away from the involved side, a large effusion with obvious signs. Tell: findings begin well before a liter, once the effusion passes 300 mL.

set1.q: In Light's criteria, which pleural-to-serum protein ratio marks an exudate?
opts: A protein ratio of 0.5 or less sits on the transudative side; an exudate needs a ratio greater than 0.5, because exudates are high-protein fluid. Tell: transudates are low-protein fluid from pressure changes, exudates high-protein fluid from permeability.

Two-thirds belongs to the third criterion: pleural fluid lactate dehydrogenase above two-thirds of the upper limit of normal serum lactate dehydrogenase. Tell: the fraction of the upper limit applies to lactate dehydrogenase, not protein.

Correct. The protein criterion is pleural fluid protein divided by serum protein greater than 0.5. An exudate is high-protein fluid that leaks out through increased vascular permeability from inflammation, and meeting this criterion alone is enough.
Greater than 0.6 is the threshold for the lactate dehydrogenase ratio, pleural fluid over serum, not the protein ratio. Tell: protein 0.5, lactate dehydrogenase 0.6.

set1.q: Which describes chemical rather than mechanical pleurodesis?
opts: Correct. Chemical pleurodesis is instillation of a sclerosant, drugs or talc, into the pleural space, performed via a chest tube or thoracoscopically. Mechanical pleurodesis is manual abrasion of the pleura performed via surgical intervention.

Manual abrasion of the pleura is mechanical pleurodesis, done surgically, as with the pleural abrasion added to bleb stapling at thoracoscopy or thoracotomy. Tell: chemical means something is instilled; mechanical means the pleura is abraded.

Stapling or resection of blebs is a procedure done at thoracoscopic surgery, often paired with pleurodesis, but it is not pleurodesis itself. Tell: stapling removes the leaking blebs, while pleurodesis seals the space.

Removing air with a needle is catheter aspiration or needle decompression, which empties the space without creating adhesions. Tell: pleurodesis leaves the layers adherent; aspiration only evacuates them.

set1.q: Which symptom is less commonly observed in primary spontaneous pneumothorax?
opts: Correct. Cough is less commonly observed in primary spontaneous pneumothorax. The usual picture is acute onset dyspnea with ipsilateral acute pleuritic chest pain, a severe stabbing pain that increases with deep breathing; a small one may be asymptomatic or cause only fatigue.

Acute onset dyspnea is one of the main symptoms of a primary spontaneous pneumothorax, not an uncommon one. Tell: the symptom singled out as less common is cough, while dyspnea and pleuritic pain lead the history.

Ipsilateral acute pleuritic chest pain, severe and stabbing and worse with deep breathing, is a defining complaint of the primary form. Tell: same-side pleuritic pain is expected; cough is the feature described as less common.

Fatigue is a listed complaint, particularly when the pneumothorax is small and otherwise asymptomatic. Tell: a small pneumothorax may cause only fatigue, while cough is the symptom described as less common.

set1.q: Besides treating the underlying condition, which treatment is listed for pleurisy?
opts: Correct. Pleurisy is treated by treating the underlying condition and with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for the inflamed parietal pleura. Diagnostic testing likewise depends on the underlying condition, because pleurisy is a symptom rather than a diagnosis.

Antibiotics treat a bacterial cause such as pneumonia or empyema, which falls under treating the underlying condition; they are not the listed treatment for pleurisy itself. Tell: the pleural inflammation gets nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.

Chemical pleurodesis instills a sclerosant to obliterate the pleural space and is used for recurrent pneumothorax or malignant effusion, not for pleural inflammation. Tell: pleurodesis creates inflammation on purpose, while pleurisy needs it calmed.

Therapeutic thoracentesis removes pleural fluid to relieve the symptoms of an effusion; pleurisy is inflamed lining, not a fluid collection to drain. Tell: pleurisy is treated with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and attention to its cause.

set1.q: A first primary spontaneous pneumothorax has an apex-to-cupola distance under 3 cm and causes minimal symptoms. Which treatment is appropriate?
opts: Thoracoscopic surgery with pleurodesis is the treatment for a recurrent primary pneumothorax, not a first small one. Tell: a first episode is managed by size and symptoms; surgery waits for recurrence.

Correct. A small primary spontaneous pneumothorax, under 3 cm at the apex, with no or minimal symptoms is observed with adequate analgesia and 100% oxygen by non-rebreather mask, which accelerates resorption of air. A repeat film in 6 to 12 hours confirms it has not expanded before discharge.

A chest tube is for a moderate or large primary pneumothorax, over 3 cm with moderate or severe symptoms, or after failed observation or aspiration. Tell: small and minimally symptomatic means watch, not drain.

Catheter aspiration is for a small primary pneumothorax with significant dyspnea after analgesia; this patient has only minimal symptoms. Tell: dyspnea that persists despite pain control is what moves a small pneumothorax to aspiration.

set1.q: What benefit does open thoracotomy offer in a complicated pneumothorax?
opts: Open thoracotomy carries the potential risks of general anesthesia, as thoracoscopic surgery does. Tell: anesthesia is a drawback shared by both operations, so avoiding it is not a benefit of either.

Correct. Thoracoscopic surgery has supplanted thoracotomy, but open thoracotomy remains valuable for complicated cases: it allows examination of the lung for the site of the air leak and enables lysis of previous adhesions. Its drawbacks are anesthesia risk, increased cost and significant discomfort.
A significant amount of patient discomfort is a listed drawback of open thoracotomy, not a benefit. Tell: the open approach trades comfort for full access to the leak and the adhesions.
Increased cost is a drawback of thoracotomy, and greater financial cost is a risk of thoracoscopic surgery too. Tell: neither operation is chosen to save money.

set1.q: What does an arterial blood gas usually show in pneumothorax?
opts: Correct. An arterial blood gas usually reveals hypoxemia and respiratory alkalosis, though results depend on ventilation status and the compensatory response. The test is often unnecessary and is kept for severe underlying lung disease or persistent respiratory distress despite treatment.
Hypoxemia fits, but the usual acid-base change reported in pneumothorax is respiratory alkalosis rather than acidosis. Tell: the typical gas pairs low oxygen with alkalosis.
Oxygen is usually low, and a metabolic acidosis is not the described pattern. Tell: the gas in pneumothorax usually shows hypoxemia with a respiratory, not metabolic, disturbance.

Neither half matches: the usual result is hypoxemia with respiratory alkalosis, and the gas is often unnecessary unless lung disease is severe or distress persists. Tell: the disturbance is respiratory, and its direction is alkalosis.

set1.q: Which feature belongs to the visceral pleura rather than the parietal pleura?
opts: Intercostal and phrenic nerve fibers give the parietal pleura its sensory innervation; the visceral pleura has none. Tell: the layer that can hurt is the parietal one, so any named sensory nerve points to the parietal pleura.

Higher hydrostatic pressure is a parietal feature that goes with its systemic blood supply; the visceral pleura has the lower hydrostatic pressure. Tell: parietal is higher pressure and systemic, visceral is lower pressure and pulmonary.

Correct. The visceral pleura covers the lungs, takes its blood from the pulmonary circulation, has the lower hydrostatic pressure and has no sensory innervation. That is why pleuritic pain comes from the parietal layer, whose pain fibers are stimulated when the two layers rub together.

A systemic blood supply belongs to the parietal pleura, which lines the thoracic cavity, diaphragm and mediastinum; the visceral pleura is supplied by the pulmonary circulation. Tell: systemic supply goes with the wall-lining layer, pulmonary supply with the lung-covering layer.

set1.q: Which pair of physical findings is expected over a pneumothorax?
opts: Correct. Over a pneumothorax, percussion is hyperresonant and tactile fremitus is decreased or absent, because pleural air impedes the transmission of vibrations from the larynx to the chest surface. Breath and voice sounds are diminished or absent on the affected side as well.

Dullness with decreased fremitus is the effusion pattern: fluid sounds dull and obstructs the transmission of vibrations. Tell: air in the pleural space percusses hyperresonant, so dullness points to fluid.

The percussion half is right, but fremitus is not increased over pleural air; transmission of vibrations is impeded, so fremitus is decreased or absent. Tell: air and fluid in the pleural space both dampen fremitus.

Neither half fits pleural air: a pneumothorax is hyperresonant, and its fremitus is decreased or absent. Tell: in a pneumothorax the transmitted vibrations and sounds are reduced on the affected side.

set1.q: What usually causes pleurodynia?
opts: Bacterial pneumonia is the usual precursor of a parapneumonic effusion and empyema. Tell: pleurodynia is viral, with tender intercostal muscles and a usually normal chest radiograph.

Correct. Pleurodynia is a viral myalgia, often caused by coxsackie B virus, an enterovirus, and typically follows an upper respiratory or gastrointestinal infection. Also called Bornholm disease, it peaks in summer and spreads mainly by the fecal-oral route.

Herpes zoster causes nerve root pain, one of the other causes of chest pain to consider after the dangerous ones. Tell: pleurodynia is an enteroviral infection of the intercostal muscles, not nerve root pain.
Tuberculosis is the leading cause of exudative effusion worldwide and brings fever, night sweats, hemoptysis and weight loss. Tell: pleurodynia is a viral myalgia with a usually normal chest film.

set1.q: By which mechanism does heart failure cause a pleural effusion?
opts: Reduced intravascular oncotic pressure is how hypoalbuminemia from nephrotic syndrome or cirrhosis causes an effusion. Tell: low albumin lowers oncotic pressure; a failing heart raises hydrostatic pressure.
Increased capillary permeability comes from trauma, malignancy, inflammation and infection and produces a high-protein exudate. Tell: leaky capillaries make exudates; heart failure makes transudates.

Decreased lymphatic drainage or complete lymphatic blockage is the mechanism of effusion from malignancy or trauma. Tell: blocked outflow is a lymph problem; heart failure is a pressure problem in the capillaries.

Correct. Heart failure causes effusion through increased capillary hydrostatic pressure, which moves fluid across a membrane and produces a low-protein transudate. Normally fluid enters the pleural space from parietal pleural capillaries and is removed via parietal pleural lymphatics.

set1.q: Which examination finding separates a pleural effusion from a pneumothorax?
opts: Tactile fremitus is decreased in both conditions: fluid obstructs the transmission of vibrations, and pleural air impedes it too. Tell: a finding shared by both cannot tell them apart.
Diminished or absent breath sounds occur over an effusion and on the side of a pneumothorax alike. Tell: percussion, dull or hyperresonant, is what separates fluid from air.
Hyperresonance is the pneumothorax note; over an effusion, percussion is dull. Tell: a hollow, hyperresonant side holds air, and a dull side holds fluid.

Correct. Percussion separates them: an effusion is dull over the fluid, while a pneumothorax is hyperresonant. Both decrease tactile fremitus and diminish breath sounds on the affected side, because fluid and air each obstruct the transmission of vibrations and sound.

set1.q: What advantage does a Heimlich valve offer a patient with a pneumothorax?
opts: A Heimlich valve is one-way: air leaves the chest but cannot return. Tell: a valve that let air back in would recreate the pneumothorax it is meant to drain.

Correct. A Heimlich valve is a one-way flutter valve attached to a tube inserted in the chest, open to air or attached to a drainage bag. The device is small and portable, which promotes ambulation; it is listed with chest tube insertion for a small primary pneumothorax with significant dyspnea.

Preventing recurrence is the job of pleurodesis, or thoracoscopic surgery with pleurodesis, which obliterate the pleural space. Tell: the valve only lets air out; it does nothing to stop a future pneumothorax.
The valve drains air one way and repairs nothing; a persistent air leak is a reason for thoracoscopic surgery. Tell: one-way flutter means drainage, not closure of the leak.

set1.q: Which complication can follow a retained hemothorax?
opts: Pneumomediastinum is air in the mediastinal tissues from ruptured alveoli or an esophageal or bowel perforation; it does not follow retained blood. Tell: undrained blood becomes a nidus for infection, so the answer is empyema.

Pleurodynia is a viral myalgia of the intercostal muscles, usually from coxsackie B virus, unrelated to blood in the pleural space. Tell: a retained hemothorax leads to empyema, fibrothorax and trapped lung.

Correct. Undrained blood collections serve as a primary nidus for infection, and a retained hemothorax directly leads to empyema, fibrothorax and trapped lung. That is why chest tube placement is the essential first step for drainage.

Chylothorax is chyle in the pleural space from thoracic duct disruption, most often after trauma such as thoracic surgery, not a result of retained blood. Tell: milky fluid means chyle; retained blood leads to infection and scarring.

set1.q: How is a spontaneous pneumothorax classified in a tall, thin patient with Marfan syndrome?
opts: Tall, thin young males are the classic primary profile, but primary means no underlying abnormality, and Marfan syndrome is one. Tell: once a connective tissue disease is present, the pneumothorax is secondary, whatever the body type.
A traumatic pneumothorax needs a history of blunt or penetrating thoracic trauma, which is not given here. Tell: no injury means spontaneous, and the only open question is primary versus secondary.
ruled out by a stated finding

An iatrogenic pneumothorax follows a medical intervention such as thoracentesis or subclavian vein catheter placement, and none is described. Tell: Marfan syndrome is a disease, not a procedure, so it points to secondary spontaneous.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Marfan syndrome is a connective tissue disease, and connective tissue disease is listed among the underlying abnormalities of secondary spontaneous pneumothorax. The tall, thin build fits the primary profile, but the underlying disorder makes the event secondary.

set1.q: How many of Light's criteria must a pleural fluid meet to be classified as an exudate?
opts: The protein ratio is one of the three criteria, but either lactate dehydrogenase criterion counts just as much. Tell: any single criterion, protein or lactate dehydrogenase, makes the fluid an exudate.

Correct. An exudate meets at least one of Light's criteria: pleural-to-serum protein ratio above 0.5, pleural-to-serum lactate dehydrogenase ratio above 0.6, or pleural fluid lactate dehydrogenase above two-thirds of the upper limit of normal serum lactate dehydrogenase. A transudate meets none of them.
Requiring two criteria would misclassify exudates that meet a single one; any one criterion is enough. Tell: Light's criteria work as an 'any one' rule.

Requiring all three describes the wrong side of the rule: a transudate is defined by all of Light's criteria being absent, and one present criterion makes an exudate. Tell: one met, exudate; none met, transudate.

set1.q: Where is the needle placed for needle decompression of a tension pneumothorax?
opts: The midaxillary line belongs to the chest tube site in the 4th or 5th intercostal space; the 2nd-space needle goes in at the midclavicular line. Tell: the needle sits high and in front, the tube lower and to the side.
The needle goes in on the thoracic side of the pneumothorax; the opposite side is where the mediastinum has been pushed. Tell: decompress the side with the trapped air.
Under the third rib, midclavicular line
The needle passes over the 3rd rib, in the 2nd intercostal space, not under it. Tell: 'over the 3rd rib' is written into the site, the same landmark used for catheter aspiration.

Correct. The typical needle decompression site is on the thoracic side of the pneumothorax, in the 2nd intercostal space, over the 3rd rib, at the midclavicular line. Patient body habitus can change the choice, which is why this is called the typical site.

Pneumothorax 3. Spontaneous 4. Traumatic 5. Hemothorax 6. Chylothorax 7. Pleural effusion 8. Pneumomediastinum 9. Pleurodynia 10. Pleurisy 11. Empyema
set1.q: Which pair of findings fits a tension pneumothorax?
opts: Hypotension fits, but palpable subcutaneous emphysema in the neck is the finding of pneumomediastinum, with the Hamman crunch. Tell: tension shows itself in the trachea and the neck veins, not as air under the skin.
Neither half fits: the neck veins distend in tension, and the listed signs are hypotension, tracheal deviation and absent breath sounds, not a slow pulse. Tell: distended, not flat, neck veins.

Correct. In a tension pneumothorax the mediastinum shifts to the contralateral side, venous return and cardiac output fall, and the patient shows hypotension, tracheal deviation and neck vein distention, with decreased or absent breath sounds. Those bedside signs are enough to act on.
Tracheal deviation fits, but blood pressure falls rather than rises, because decreased venous return lowers cardiac output. Tell: tension lowers the blood pressure.

Pneumothorax 3. Spontaneous 4. Traumatic 5. Hemothorax 6. Chylothorax 7. Pleural effusion 8. Pneumomediastinum 9. Pleurodynia 10. Pleurisy 11. Empyema
set1.q: When counseling patients after a spontaneous pneumothorax, which group needs early surgical evaluation for safety?
opts: Office work carries no stated recurrence danger and is not a reason for early surgery. Tell: early surgical evaluation targets the groups for whom a recurrence would be dangerous, pilots and divers.
Running is not named as a reason for early surgery, and a primary pneumothorax often occurs at rest anyway. Tell: the safety referral is for pilots and divers.

Quitting tobacco lowers the recurrence risk, so a former smoker is not singled out for early surgery. Tell: smoking cessation is advice for every patient; early surgical evaluation is for pilots and divers.

Correct. Pilots and divers need early surgical options for safety: high-pressure activities such as diving carry severe recurrence dangers, and scuba diving is to be avoided. Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery closes leaks to prevent future collapses.

Pneumothorax 3. Spontaneous 4. Traumatic 5. Hemothorax 6. Chylothorax 7. Pleural effusion 8. Pneumomediastinum 9. Pleurodynia 10. Pleurisy 11. Empyema
set1.q: What is the initial imaging test for a suspected pneumothorax in a stable patient?
opts: A supine film is what a patient lying flat gets, and there a pneumothorax may show only as a deep sulcus sign at the costophrenic angle. Tell: a stable patient gets the standard upright film, where the visceral pleural line is seen.

An arterial blood gas is often unnecessary in pneumothorax and is reserved for severe underlying lung disease or persistent distress despite treatment. Tell: a blood gas measures the effect, while the upright film shows the air.

Correct. The initial test for pneumothorax is a standard upright chest radiograph, which establishes the diagnosis by showing the visceral pleural line. It serves as rapid initial triage for the upright, symptomatic patient; computed tomography is the gold standard but is not the first test.

Chest computed tomography is the diagnostic gold standard and best for presence, size and location, but it is impractical when time is critical and is not the initial test. Tell: do not confuse gold standard with best initial test.

Pneumothorax 3. Spontaneous 4. Traumatic 5. Hemothorax 6. Chylothorax 7. Pleural effusion 8. Pneumomediastinum 9. Pleurodynia 10. Pleurisy 11. Empyema
set1.q: After needle decompression of a tension pneumothorax, which step follows?
opts: Observation with oxygen suits a small, minimally symptomatic primary pneumothorax, not a tension pneumothorax that has just been decompressed. Tell: after the needle comes the tube, then admission.
Catheter aspiration is contraindicated in tension pneumothorax and in hemodynamic instability. Tell: the step after needle decompression is a moderate or large chest tube.
ruled out by a stated finding

Chemical pleurodesis prevents recurrence and is not part of emergency management; it is used, for example, through a chest tube when surgery is not an option in secondary disease. Tell: emergency care is needle, then chest tube, then admission.

Correct. Needle decompression is followed by moderate or large-size chest tube insertion and admission; immediate chest tube placement would have been ideal had a tube been readily available. The needle relieves the tension, and the chest tube then drains the pleural space.

set1.q: About how much fluid does the normal pleural cavity contain?
opts: Correct. The pleural cavity is a potential space that contains about 10 mL of fluid, roughly 2 teaspoons. That thin film lubricates the layers and maintains coupling of the lung with the chest wall; fluid inflow from the parietal capillaries equals reabsorption by the parietal lymphatics.

About 75 mL is the amount of pleural fluid that blunts the posterior costophrenic angle on an upright chest radiograph, so it is already an effusion. Tell: the normal space holds only about 2 teaspoons, about 10 mL.
Effusions smaller than 300 mL produce no physical exam findings, which makes 300 mL an effusion threshold rather than a normal volume. Tell: normal pleural fluid is a thin film of about 10 mL.

More than 1000 mL of effusion can shift the trachea away from the involved side, a large effusion far beyond the normal film of about 10 mL. Tell: a liter is a tracheal-shift volume, not a normal one.

set1.q: What is the most common cause of chylothorax?
opts: Correct. Chylothorax is thoracic duct disruption that lets lipid from chyle, lymph fluid, collect in the pleural space; trauma, for example thoracic surgery, is the most common cause, and tumors in the mediastinum are the other. Without obvious trauma, a lymphangiogram and computed tomography assess the mediastinum.
Mediastinal tumors are the other listed cause, the one to look for with a lymphangiogram and computed tomography when there is no obvious trauma. Tell: trauma, often surgical, comes first.
Bacterial pneumonia with a parapneumonic effusion is the most common precursor of empyema, not of chylothorax. Tell: pus follows pneumonia; chyle follows thoracic duct injury.
Heart failure produces a transudate by raising capillary hydrostatic pressure; it does not disrupt the thoracic duct. Tell: milky chyle in the pleural space means the duct was injured.

Pneumothorax 3. Spontaneous 4. Traumatic 5. Hemothorax 6. Chylothorax 7. Pleural effusion 8. Pneumomediastinum 9. Pleurodynia 10. Pleurisy 11. Empyema
set1.q: A secondary spontaneous pneumothorax needs recurrence prevention, but surgery is not an option. What is used instead?
opts: Observation treats a small asymptomatic episode; it does not lower the high recurrence risk of secondary disease. Tell: preventing recurrence without surgery means chemical pleurodesis.

Correct. Most secondary spontaneous pneumothoraces are treated with a chest tube and may go on to thoracoscopic surgery or thoracotomy with bleb stapling and pleural abrasion; if surgery is not an option, chemical pleurodesis is performed via the chest tube. The sclerosant obliterates the space without an operation.

Thoracotomy with pleural abrasion is mechanical pleurodesis, and it is surgery, which this patient cannot have. Tell: when surgery is ruled out, the sclerosant goes in through the existing chest tube.
ruled out by a stated finding

Catheter aspiration is contraindicated with underlying pulmonary disease and with recurrent pneumothorax, and it does nothing to prevent recurrence. Tell: prevention needs pleurodesis, which here is chemical, via the tube.
ruled out by a stated finding

set1.q: What causes a pleural effusion to become loculated?
opts: Correct. Loculations are fluid-filled compartments within the pleural space that occur when there are adhesions between the visceral and parietal pleurae. They go with conditions that cause pleural inflammation, such as empyema, and the fluid stays stuck in a pocket instead of layering freely.
Raised hydrostatic pressure, as in heart failure, produces a transudate; it does not create compartments. Tell: loculation needs inflammation and the adhesions it leaves.
Thoracic duct disruption explains what the fluid is, chyle, not why it is divided into pockets. Tell: compartments come from adhesions between the visceral and parietal pleura.
Air above fluid with a straight line and no meniscus is a hemopneumothorax, not a loculated effusion. Tell: loculations are compartments of fluid separated by adhesions.

set1.q: Which history can precede a spontaneous pneumomediastinum?
opts: Heart failure raises capillary hydrostatic pressure and causes a pleural effusion. Tell: pneumomediastinum comes from a sudden rise in intrathoracic pressure, such as violent coughing, not from fluid overload.

Correct. Spontaneous pneumomediastinum may follow a sudden increase in intrathoracic pressure, such as violent coughing, vomiting or inhalation drug use with a Valsalva maneuver. Excessive intra-alveolar pressure ruptures alveoli bordering the mediastinum, and air collects in the mediastinal tissues.

Coxsackie B virus causes pleurodynia, a viral myalgia of the intercostal muscles with a raised creatine kinase, not air in the mediastinum. Tell: pneumomediastinum follows a pressure surge, not an infection.
Thoracic duct disruption lets chyle collect in the pleural space, a chylothorax. Tell: a ruptured lymph channel leaks milky fluid; ruptured alveoli leak air.

set1.q: Which option lets a patient with a short prognosis and a recurrent malignant effusion drain fluid at home?
opts: Therapeutic thoracentesis relieves symptoms, but each tap is a separate procedure rather than drainage at home. Tell: minimizing hospital time for a short prognosis points to the tunneled catheter.
Thoracoscopic surgery is an operation with the risks of general anesthesia and greater cost, not a home drainage method. Tell: draining at home between visits is the job of the tunneled catheter.

Correct. An indwelling tunneled pleural catheter is placed in the outpatient setting and intermittently drained at home, which minimizes time in hospital for patients with short prognoses. It runs through a one-way valve to a negative-pressure bottle.
Chemical pleurodesis is instilled through a chest tube to obliterate the space; it is not drained at home. Tell: home drainage means the tunneled catheter.

set1.q: Where is a chest tube most commonly inserted?
opts: The 2nd intercostal space at the midclavicular line is the typical needle decompression and catheter aspiration site; a chest tube goes there only for the less common anterior access in a pneumothorax. Tell: the needle sits high and in front, the usual tube lower and to the side.
The 4th or 5th space is right, but the line is wrong: the tube goes in at the midaxillary line, on the side of the chest. Tell: the midclavicular line belongs with the 2nd-space needle site.
The 2nd intercostal space pairs with the midclavicular line, for needle decompression, not with the midaxillary line. Tell: the usual chest tube pairs the 4th or 5th space with the midaxillary line.

Correct. The most common chest tube site is the fourth or fifth intercostal space at the midaxillary line. Chest tube thoracostomy places the tube to drain fluid or air from the pleural space, for pneumothorax or pleural effusion.

set2.q: A first primary spontaneous pneumothorax has an apex-to-cupola distance greater than 3 cm with significant dyspnea and chest pain. Which treatment is listed?
opts: Thoracoscopic surgery with pleurodesis is the treatment when a primary pneumothorax recurs, and this is a first episode. Tell: first and large means chest tube; recurrent means surgery with pleurodesis.
Open thoracotomy is kept for complicated cases, and thoracoscopic surgery has largely supplanted it. Tell: an uncomplicated first large pneumothorax is drained with a chest tube, not opened.

Correct. A moderate or large primary spontaneous pneumothorax, more than 3 cm at the apex, with moderate or severe symptoms such as significant chest pain and dyspnea, is treated with chest tube insertion. A recurrent primary pneumothorax instead goes to thoracoscopic surgery with pleurodesis.
Observation with oxygen fits a small pneumothorax, under 3 cm, with no or minimal symptoms. Tell: large size plus significant symptoms takes observation off the table.

set2.q: What does thoracentesis typically show in chylothorax?
opts: Purulent material on thoracentesis diagnoses empyema, the infected effusion that most often follows bacterial pneumonia with a parapneumonic effusion. Tell: pus is empyema; milky fluid is chyle.
Bloody fluid with a hematocrit above 50% of the peripheral blood hematocrit is a hemothorax, most often from trauma. Tell: red means blood; milky white means chyle.
Clear or straw-colored fluid usually means a transudative effusion, such as from heart failure, though appearance alone is not diagnostic. Tell: chylothorax fluid is milky white.

Correct. Thoracentesis in chylothorax shows milky fluid with elevated triglycerides, reflecting lipid from chyle that has leaked through a disrupted thoracic duct. On the pleural fluid color guide, milky white means chylothorax.

set2.q: A pleural fluid has a protein ratio to serum of 0.7, and both lactate dehydrogenase criteria are unmet. How is it classified?
opts: Correct. Light's criteria classify a fluid as an exudate when at least one criterion is met, and a protein ratio of 0.7 is above the 0.5 cutoff. The two unmet lactate dehydrogenase criteria do not change that, because a transudate requires all of the criteria to be absent.
A transudate needs all of Light's criteria absent, and the protein criterion is met here. Tell: the majority does not rule; a single met criterion makes an exudate.

Light's criteria leave no indeterminate zone: one or more met criteria means exudate, and all criteria absent means transudate. Tell: the rule is any one, not a vote, so the 0.7 protein ratio decides it.

Normal pleural fluid is a clear ultrafiltrate of plasma low in protein, under 1 to 2 g/dL; Light's criteria sort an effusion, not normal fluid. Tell: a protein ratio above 0.5 places an effusion with the exudates.

set2.q: Which respiratory rate is part of the American College of Chest Physicians definition of a stable patient with spontaneous pneumothorax?
opts: Twenty breaths per minute is stricter than the definition; the stability limit is a respiratory rate under 24. Tell: the stability numbers are 24 for breathing, 60 to 120 for heart rate and 90 percent for saturation.

Correct. The American College of Chest Physicians calls a patient stable only with all of: respiratory rate under 24 breaths per minute, heart rate above 60 and below 120, normal blood pressure, room-air oxygen saturation above 90 percent and the ability to speak in whole sentences. All other patients are unstable.

A rate above 30 breaths per minute is the persistent tachypnea that marks failure of observation and calls for a chest tube, well past the stability limit. Tell: 24 defines stable; 30 signals failed observation.
Thirty-six breaths per minute is far past the limit; a patient breathing 24 or more times a minute is already unstable. Tell: stability requires a respiratory rate under 24 breaths per minute.

Pneumothorax 3. Spontaneous 4. Traumatic 5. Hemothorax 6. Chylothorax 7. Pleural effusion 8. Pneumomediastinum 9. Pleurodynia 10. Pleurisy 11. Empyema
set2.q: Which underlying condition most commonly causes a secondary spontaneous pneumothorax?
opts: Interstitial lung disease, with sarcoidosis as the example, is a listed cause of secondary spontaneous pneumothorax but not the most common one. Tell: the most common is chronic obstructive disease, whose apical blebs rupture.
Connective tissue disease, with Marfan syndrome as the example, makes a pneumothorax secondary, but it is a less common cause. Tell: the leading cause is chronic obstructive lung disease.

Bronchogenic carcinoma, a lung malignancy, can cause a secondary pneumothorax and may even be its initial symptom, but it is not the most frequent cause. Tell: most common goes to chronic obstructive disease.

Correct. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, also called chronic obstructive lung disease, is the most common underlying abnormality in secondary spontaneous pneumothorax, through rupture of apical blebs. Lung malignancy, cystic fibrosis, pneumonia, tuberculosis, sarcoidosis and Marfan syndrome are other causes.

set2.q: What is the most common cause of hemothorax?
opts: Correct. Trauma is the most common cause of hemothorax, through injury to the heart or vasculature, the lung parenchyma, or the intercostal, pulmonary or internal thoracic arteries; blunt or penetrating trauma causes the majority of cases. Neoplasms are the other listed etiology.

Neoplasms are a listed cause of hemothorax, but trauma is the most common one, with blunt or penetrating injury behind the majority of cases. Tell: when blood fills the pleural space, think of injury first.

An effusion that enlarges during anticoagulation calls for thoracentesis to rule out hemothorax, but anticoagulation is not the most common cause. Tell: blunt or penetrating trauma causes the majority of cases.
A hemopneumothorax complicates 2% to 3% of spontaneous pneumothoraces, which makes spontaneous rupture an uncommon source of pleural blood. Tell: trauma, not spontaneous rupture, dominates.

Pneumothorax 3. Spontaneous 4. Traumatic 5. Hemothorax 6. Chylothorax 7. Pleural effusion 8. Pneumomediastinum 9. Pleurodynia 10. Pleurisy 11. Empyema
set2.q: Which radiographic sign suggests a pneumothorax on a supine film?
opts: A straight line with no meniscus is the air-fluid level of a hemopneumothorax, where blood lies beneath the air. Tell: a supine film of air alone shows a dark, deep costophrenic angle.

Correct. With the patient supine, pleural air collects laterally and makes the costophrenic angle dark and deep; that lucency is the deep sulcus sign. On an upright film the same air would instead show as a visceral pleural line.

A blunted costophrenic angle is fluid: 75 mL of effusion blunts the posterior angle and 175 mL the lateral angle on an upright film. Tell: a pneumothorax makes the angle darker and deeper, not blunted.

The stratosphere sign is an ultrasound M-mode finding, parallel horizontal lines replacing the normal seashore pattern, not a sign on a film. Tell: radiographs show the deep sulcus; ultrasound shows absent lung sliding and the stratosphere pattern.

Pneumothorax 3. Spontaneous 4. Traumatic 5. Hemothorax 6. Chylothorax 7. Pleural effusion 8. Pneumomediastinum 9. Pleurodynia 10. Pleurisy 11. Empyema
set2.q: Which is a risk factor for an infection-related pleural effusion?
opts: Correct. The listed risk factors for infection-related pleural effusion are diabetes, alcoholism, immunosuppression and poor dental hygiene. Infection is the second largest group of effusion causes after congestive heart failure.

Peritoneal dialysis causes effusion when peritoneal fluid leaks across the diaphragm through microperforations, a fluid-shift mechanism rather than an infection risk. Tell: the infection risks are diabetes, alcoholism, immunosuppression and poor dental hygiene.

Thoracic surgery is the usual trauma behind a chylothorax, through thoracic duct disruption. Tell: surgery injures the duct; infection risk comes from conditions such as diabetes or poor dental hygiene.

Heart failure causes effusion by raising capillary hydrostatic pressure and is the leading cause overall, but it is not an infection risk factor. Tell: the infection risks are diabetes, alcoholism, immunosuppression and dental disease.

set2.q: Catheter aspiration is contraindicated in a symptomatic pneumothorax from chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Which treatment is used instead?
opts: Needle decompression is the emergency step for a tension pneumothorax when a chest tube is not readily available. Tell: a symptomatic secondary pneumothorax without tension signs gets a chest tube directly.

Sending a symptomatic secondary pneumothorax home ignores the diminished pulmonary reserve that makes it life-threatening; even a small one is hospitalized. Tell: secondary disease stays in hospital, and symptoms mean a chest tube.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Underlying pulmonary disease is a contraindication to catheter aspiration, and most secondary spontaneous pneumothoraces are treated with chest tube insertion; a small secondary one gets a chest tube once it causes symptoms. Thoracoscopic surgery, thoracotomy or chemical pleurodesis via the tube can follow.
Observation is reserved for a small secondary pneumothorax that causes no symptoms, and even then in hospital. Tell: once a secondary pneumothorax causes symptoms, the listed step is a chest tube.

Pneumothorax 3. Spontaneous 4. Traumatic 5. Hemothorax 6. Chylothorax 7. Pleural effusion 8. Pneumomediastinum 9. Pleurodynia 10. Pleurisy 11. Empyema
set2.q: Pleurisy is inflammation of which structure?
opts: Inflammation or necrosis of the striated intercostal muscles describes pleurodynia, a viral myalgia usually from coxsackie B virus, with a raised creatine kinase. Tell: muscle inflammation is pleurodynia; inflammation of the pleural lining is pleurisy.

Correct. Pleurisy is inflammation of the parietal pleura: the pleural layers rub together and stimulate the pain fibers of the parietal pleura, causing pleuritic pain. It is a symptom rather than a diagnosis, so the condition underneath still has to be found and treated.

The visceral pleura covers the lungs and has no sensory innervation, so its inflammation could not produce the sharp, localized pain of pleurisy. Tell: pain needs nerve fibers, and only the parietal pleura has them, from the intercostal and phrenic nerves.

Pericarditis is a separate dangerous cause of chest pain to consider immediately, and its friction rub persists when the breath is held. Tell: a rub that disappears with breath holding is pleural, from the parietal pleura.

Pneumothorax 3. Spontaneous 4. Traumatic 5. Hemothorax 6. Chylothorax 7. Pleural effusion 8. Pneumomediastinum 9. Pleurodynia 10. Pleurisy 11. Empyema
set2.q: When counseling a patient after a first spontaneous pneumothorax, what recurrence risk within three years should be quoted?
opts: Five percent badly understates the risk; recurrence approaches 50% within three years of a first spontaneous pneumothorax. Tell: recurrence is common, which is why prevention belongs in the discharge talk.
Ten percent understates it; about half of patients will have another spontaneous pneumothorax within three years. Tell: the number to give is 50% within three years.

Correct. Patient education after a spontaneous pneumothorax explains the condition and warns that recurrence approaches 50% within three years after an initial episode. The best preventive procedure is video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery with pleurodesis, and smoking cessation should be discussed.

Over 75% is the share of recurrent pneumothoraces that occur on the original side, a different figure from the risk of recurring at all. Tell: 50% within three years is the risk; the same-side figure describes where recurrences happen.

Pneumothorax 3. Spontaneous 4. Traumatic 5. Hemothorax 6. Chylothorax 7. Pleural effusion 8. Pneumomediastinum 9. Pleurodynia 10. Pleurisy 11. Empyema
set2.q: What does pleurodesis do to the pleural space?
opts: Correct. Pleurodesis obliterates the pleural space by inducing intrapleural inflammation: an irritant causes adhesions of the two pleural layers. That keeps the lung inflated after a pneumothorax and leaves no room for additional fluid to accumulate in a pleural effusion.
Pleurodesis leaves no room for additional fluid; the adhesions remove the space where fluid would collect. Tell: the goal is a sealed space, not more lubrication.
The point is the opposite: the irritant makes the two layers adhere so the space is obliterated. Tell: after pleurodesis the layers are joined by adhesions, which is what keeps the lung inflated.

Continuous drainage is what a chest tube does, removing air or fluid from the pleural space. Tell: pleurodesis does not drain; it seals the space with adhesions, and the sclerosant is often instilled through a chest tube.

Pneumothorax 3. Spontaneous 4. Traumatic 5. Hemothorax 6. Chylothorax 7. Pleural effusion 8. Pneumomediastinum 9. Pleurodynia 10. Pleurisy 11. Empyema
set2.q: How is uncomplicated pneumomediastinum managed after the airway is secured?
opts: Needle decompression relieves a tension pneumothorax when a chest tube is not readily available. Tell: pneumomediastinum has no trapped pleural air to decompress; it is managed conservatively.

Correct. After the airway is assessed and maintained and any identified cause is treated, pneumomediastinum is managed conservatively: the air is often gradually absorbed, oxygen may increase absorption, and the patient avoids physical activity and takes analgesics. A severe case gets an emergent cardiothoracic surgery consult.

Surgery is not the default; a severe pneumomediastinum prompts an emergent cardiothoracic surgery consult, while an uncomplicated one does not. Tell: uncomplicated mediastinal air is usually absorbed on its own.
A chest tube drains air or fluid from the pleural space, for pneumothorax or effusion; mediastinal air is not in the pleural space. Tell: air in the mediastinum is usually left to absorb.

Pneumothorax 3. Spontaneous 4. Traumatic 5. Hemothorax 6. Chylothorax 7. Pleural effusion 8. Pneumomediastinum 9. Pleurodynia 10. Pleurisy 11. Empyema
set2.q: In a tension pneumothorax, what is done immediately if a chest tube is not readily available?
opts: Tension pneumothorax is a listed contraindication to catheter aspiration, as is hemodynamic instability. Tell: the emergency needle for tension is needle decompression, also called needle thoracostomy.
ruled out by a stated finding
There is no time for the X-ray: tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis and a medical emergency. Tell: a film before decompression is the delay the diagnosis warns against.

A Heimlich valve is a one-way flutter valve attached to a tube already inserted in the chest, used for portable drainage, not emergency decompression. Tell: without a chest tube there is nothing to attach the valve to.

Correct. Immediate chest tube placement is ideal for a tension pneumothorax; if a chest tube is not readily available, immediate needle decompression is performed, followed by a moderate or large-size chest tube and admission.

Pneumothorax 3. Spontaneous 4. Traumatic 5. Hemothorax 6. Chylothorax 7. Pleural effusion 8. Pneumomediastinum 9. Pleurodynia 10. Pleurisy 11. Empyema
set2.q: Which feature separates a primary from a secondary spontaneous pneumothorax?
opts: Size, from the apex-to-cupola distance, sorts small from large and guides treatment, but it does not classify the cause. Tell: primary versus secondary asks about the lung underneath, not about the amount of air.

Correct. Both kinds of spontaneous pneumothorax occur without thoracic trauma; the primary form has no underlying lung abnormality, while the secondary form has one, chronic obstructive lung disease most commonly. Primary patients usually have good pulmonary reserve.

Absence of thoracic trauma is what makes a pneumothorax spontaneous at all, so it is shared by the primary and secondary forms. Tell: the split between primary and secondary is whether the lung itself is diseased.

A primary spontaneous pneumothorax often occurs at rest but may occur during strenuous exercise, and the activity at onset does not define the type. Tell: classification depends on underlying lung disease, not on what the patient was doing.

Pneumothorax 3. Spontaneous 4. Traumatic 5. Hemothorax 6. Chylothorax 7. Pleural effusion 8. Pneumomediastinum 9. Pleurodynia 10. Pleurisy 11. Empyema
set2.q: How does pleurodynia often present in children, compared with adults?
opts: Pleuritic chest pain is how adults present; children more often have abdominal pain. Tell: the age split in pleurodynia is chest in adults, abdomen in children.
Ipsilateral shoulder or neck pain is referred pain from pleurisy of the central diaphragm through the phrenic nerve. Tell: pleurodynia in children shows up in the abdomen.
Pleurodynia is painful by definition, with paroxysms of severe, knife-like pain alongside the fever. Tell: in children the pain is felt in the abdomen.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Pleurodynia brings acute onset of fever with pleuritic pain in adults or abdominal pain in children, in paroxysms of severe, knife-like pain lasting 15 to 30 minutes with sweating and tachypnea. The involved muscles are usually tender.

set2.q: Which apex-to-cupola distance separates a small from a large pneumothorax in the American College of Chest Physicians system?
opts: One centimeter is the size that separates a bleb, under 1 cm, from a bulla, over 1 cm, not a small from a large pneumothorax. Tell: pneumothorax size uses the 3 cm apex-to-cupola line.

Two centimeters is not the threshold in this system; the apex-to-cupola cutoff is 3 cm. Tell: one number for size, 3 cm at the apex, sorts observation from chest tube in a symptomatic primary pneumothorax.

Correct. The American College of Chest Physicians defines pneumothorax size by the apex-to-cupola distance, with a distance under 3 cm called small and larger distances called large. That one number then sorts the treatment of primary and secondary spontaneous pneumothorax.

Five centimeters would label many large pneumothoraces small; the American College of Chest Physicians line is drawn at 3 cm from apex to cupola. Tell: a primary pneumothorax beyond 3 cm with moderate or severe symptoms already needs a chest tube.

set2.q: Which is an indication for video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery in pneumothorax?
opts: A small first primary spontaneous pneumothorax is observed or, with significant dyspnea after analgesia, aspirated; surgery waits for recurrence or failure. Tell: thoracoscopic surgery answers repeat or complicated events, not an uncomplicated first one.
Tension pneumothorax is an emergency treated with a chest tube or immediate needle decompression, not an operation. Tell: there is no time for surgery; tension needs decompression at the bedside.

Uncomplicated pneumomediastinum is treated conservatively, because mediastinal air is often gradually absorbed; only a severe case prompts an emergent cardiothoracic surgery consult. Tell: thoracoscopic surgery is listed for pleural problems, not for simple mediastinal air.

Correct. Thoracoscopic surgery is indicated for recurrences of spontaneous pneumothorax, bilateral pneumothorax, failure of tube thoracostomy (the lung fails to expand or an air leak persists) and secondary pneumothorax, because of its high recurrence rates and the greater consequences of recurrence.

set2.q: When is chest computed tomography impractical for a pneumothorax?
opts: Correct. Thoracic computed tomography is the best test for presence, size and location of a pneumothorax, but it is impractical in a time-critical situation. A tension pneumothorax, for example, is a clinical diagnosis with no time even for the X-ray.
Detecting blebs and bullae is one of the things computed tomography does well, so suspected blebs are a reason to use it. Tell: the scan's drawback is time, not what it can show.

Computed tomography is the best modality for determining size, as well as presence and location. Tell: when size matters and the patient is stable, the scan is useful; when time is short, it is impractical.
Computed tomography assesses underlying lung disease, which matters in a secondary pneumothorax. Tell: the scan is impractical only when the clock is the problem.

set2.q: Pleurisy of the central diaphragm refers pain to the ipsilateral shoulder or neck through which nerve fibers?
opts: Intercostal fibers supply the parietal pleura of the chest wall, which is why most pleuritic pain is well localized over the chest wall itself. Tell: pain felt away from the chest, in the shoulder or neck, travels on the phrenic fibers of the central diaphragm.

The vagus nerve is not among the sensory nerves of the pleura; the parietal pleura's sensory innervation is intercostal and phrenic nerve fibers. Tell: shoulder or neck pain from the central diaphragm follows the phrenic fibers.
The visceral pleura has no sensory innervation at all, so it cannot carry referred pain. Tell: every pleuritic pain, local or referred, starts in the parietal pleura, here through the phrenic nerve.

Correct. The parietal pleura on the central diaphragm is innervated by phrenic nerve fibers, so inflammation there may cause ipsilateral, same-side, shoulder or neck pain. Elsewhere the parietal pleura has intercostal fibers, which give well-localized, sharp chest wall pain.

set2.q: Which pneumothorax is a contraindication to catheter aspiration?
opts: A first primary episode is where aspiration fits; recurrence, not a first event, is on the contraindication list. Tell: recurrent, bilateral, traumatic and tension pneumothoraces are the exclusions.

A small primary spontaneous pneumothorax with significant dyspnea after analgesia is the listed indication for catheter aspiration. Tell: an indication cannot also be the contraindication; bilateral disease is excluded.

Good pulmonary reserve describes the primary patient without underlying lung disease, who can be aspirated; underlying pulmonary disease is the contraindication. Tell: healthy lungs permit aspiration, diseased lungs do not.

Correct. Catheter aspiration is contraindicated in bilateral pneumothoraces, and also in traumatic, tension and recurrent pneumothorax, hemodynamic instability, underlying pulmonary disease and bleeding disorders. Its place is a small primary pneumothorax with significant dyspnea after analgesia.

set2.q: Needle decompression of a tension pneumothorax is also known as what?
opts: Thoracentesis removes pleural fluid, diagnostically or therapeutically, from an effusion. Tell: thoracentesis is for fluid; decompressing trapped air in tension is a needle thoracostomy.

Catheter aspiration uses a large-gauge needle on a catheter with a stopcock and syringe for a small primary pneumothorax, and tension is a contraindication to it. Tell: same landmark, different procedure and different patient.

Correct. Needle decompression, also known as needle thoracostomy, is insertion of a needle into the pleural space to decompress a tension pneumothorax, typically in the 2nd intercostal space, over the 3rd rib, at the midclavicular line.
Tube thoracostomy is chest tube placement to drain fluid or air, the step that follows needle decompression. Tell: needle thoracostomy is the temporary needle; tube thoracostomy is the chest tube.

set2.q: What is the leading cause of pleural effusion overall?
opts: Pneumonia is the most common cause of exudative effusion, but exudates are only part of the total, and heart failure leads all effusions. Tell: the most common exudate is pneumonia; the most common effusion is heart failure.

Cirrhosis with ascites causes effusion through low oncotic pressure and peritoneal fluid leaking across the diaphragm, far less often than heart failure. Tell: heart failure alone accounts for more than 90% of transudates.
Correct. Congestive heart failure is the leading cause of pleural effusion, through increased capillary hydrostatic pressure, and it accounts for more than 90% of transudative effusions.
Malignancy is a frequent cause and the second most common cause of exudative effusion, but heart failure leads overall. Tell: heart failure outnumbers every other cause of effusion.

set2.q: In Light's criteria, pleural fluid lactate dehydrogenase above what fraction of the upper limit of normal serum lactate dehydrogenase marks an exudate?
opts: Three-quarters sets the bar too high; any value above two-thirds of the upper limit of normal serum lactate dehydrogenase qualifies. Tell: the fraction in the criterion is two-thirds.

Correct. The third criterion is pleural fluid lactate dehydrogenase greater than two-thirds of the upper limit of normal serum lactate dehydrogenase. The other two are the protein ratio above 0.5 and the lactate dehydrogenase ratio above 0.6; meeting any one marks an exudate.

Normal pleural fluid has a lactate dehydrogenase under 50% of plasma, but the exudate cutoff is two-thirds of the upper limit of normal serum. Tell: one-half describes normal fluid; two-thirds is the exudate threshold.

One-third would label far more fluids as exudates than the rule does; the criterion is greater than two-thirds of the upper limit of normal serum lactate dehydrogenase. Tell: the fraction is two-thirds.

set2.q: When is a diagnostic thoracentesis performed?
opts: Routine thoracentesis for every effusion seen on a film is not the indication; it is reserved for a new effusion without a clinical cause. Tell: the question is whether the cause is already known.
A new effusion with no clinical cause

Correct. Diagnostic thoracentesis removes 50 to 100 mL of fluid for visualization and analysis and is performed when there is a new pleural effusion with no clinical cause. Therapeutic thoracentesis, by contrast, removes fluid to relieve symptoms.
An effusion explained by heart failure

An effusion with a clear clinical cause such as heart failure is managed by treating that disorder, with diuretics as the initial treatment for heart failure transudates. Tell: the effusion to sample is the one with no explanation.
ruled out by a stated finding
Imaging comes first: an upright chest radiograph shows the effusion, and ultrasound is used to guide the thoracentesis. Tell: thoracentesis follows imaging; it does not replace it.

set2.q: Which traumatic pneumothorax has a direct chest-wall wound that lets air into the pleural space during inhalation?
opts: Correct. An open pneumothorax has a direct wound in the chest wall that allows air to enter the pleural space during inhalation and can lead to a sucking chest wound. A closed pneumothorax has no external wound: air enters from the lung through broken ribs or internal injuries.
A closed pneumothorax has no external wound: air reaches the pleural space from the lung, through broken ribs or internal injuries. Tell: a hole in the chest wall makes it open.

An iatrogenic pneumothorax follows a medical intervention such as thoracentesis or subclavian vein catheter placement, not a traumatic chest-wall wound. Tell: open versus closed is the split inside traumatic pneumothorax.

A hemopneumothorax is blood and air together in the pleural space, seen on film as a straight line with no meniscus. Tell: the stem describes how air enters, through the wall, which defines an open pneumothorax.

set2.q: Why does a secondary spontaneous pneumothorax need more immediate intervention than a primary one?
opts: Size is graded the same way in both forms, by the apex-to-cupola distance, and even a small secondary pneumothorax is admitted for monitoring. Tell: the same amount of air matters more when the lung underneath has less reserve.

Correct. Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax is a more serious event because the underlying lung disease leaves diminished pulmonary reserve, which can be life-threatening and requires more immediate intervention. The symptoms are the same as in the primary form but generally greater.

Rupture of apical blebs is the shared mechanism, seen in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and in primary disease alike; it is not what makes the secondary form dangerous. Tell: the danger lies in the patient's lack of reserve, not in the bleb.

Bilateral pneumothorax is an indication for thoracoscopic surgery and a contraindication to catheter aspiration, but it is not described as typical of the secondary form. Tell: the reason given for urgency is diminished pulmonary reserve.

set2.q: In which age range does primary spontaneous pneumothorax classically occur?
opts: Correct. Primary spontaneous pneumothorax is classically a disease of tall, thin young males aged 20 to 40 years, with males affected more than females. Smoking is a significant risk factor, and these patients typically have good pulmonary reserve, so severe distress is not common.

The 40 to 60 year range sits above the classic window; primary spontaneous pneumothorax clusters in young adults, 20 to 40 years old. Tell: the primary profile is young, tall and thin, with good pulmonary reserve.

This range does not match the classic primary window of 20 to 40 years. A spontaneous pneumothorax in a patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or lung malignancy is secondary, with less reserve. Tell: primary means young adults with healthy lungs.

Primary spontaneous pneumothorax is described in young adults, 20 to 40 years, not in the very old. Tell: classic primary patients have good pulmonary reserve, which is why severe respiratory distress is uncommon in them.

set2.q: Which imaging test is the diagnostic gold standard for pneumothorax?
opts: Correct. Thoracic computed tomography is the diagnostic gold standard: it is the best modality for determining presence, size and location of a pneumothorax, assesses underlying disease, and detects blebs and bullae. It is impractical in a time-critical situation.
The standard upright chest radiograph is the initial test, used for rapid triage, but it is not the gold standard. Tell: do not confuse best initial test with gold standard.

Lung ultrasound is a rapid bedside tool, helpful in the unstable patient, but it does not assess size and is not the gold standard. Tell: the gold standard gives presence, size and location, which ultrasound cannot.

The lateral decubitus film, taken lying on the side with the effusion down, shows small amounts of layering pleural fluid and has been replaced by ultrasound. Tell: decubitus films belong to effusion, not to pneumothorax.

set2.q: Which disorder accounts for more than 90% of transudative pleural effusions?
opts: Nephrotic syndrome causes a transudate through hypoalbuminemia and reduced oncotic pressure, a much smaller group. Tell: the dominant transudate cause is a failing heart.
Peritoneal dialysis fluid can cross the diaphragm through microperforations and form a transudate, but it is an uncommon cause. Tell: heart failure accounts for more than 90%.

Correct. Congestive heart failure accounts for more than 90% of transudative effusions, through increased capillary hydrostatic pressure. Cirrhosis with ascites, nephrotic syndrome and peritoneal dialysis are other listed causes; a transudate is low-protein fluid with all of Light's criteria absent.
Cirrhosis with ascites causes transudates through low oncotic pressure and peritoneal fluid crossing the diaphragm, but it is a minor share. Tell: more than 90% belongs to heart failure.
